summary: Chagas disease is a serious infection caused by the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi, affecting millions of people mainly in Latin America. This disease can cause different health problems, especially heart disease, but it is not fully understood how different types of the parasite relate to the symptoms people develop. In this study, researchers examined blood samples from 65 patients with chronic Chagas disease in Brazil to identify the specific parasite types (called discrete typing units or DTUs) and measure how many parasites were in their blood. They used advanced DNA tests to detect and classify the parasites directly from the patients' blood. About half of the patients had detectable parasite levels, with older patients (over 70 years) showing higher amounts. The most common parasite types found were TcVI and TcII, with some patients infected by more than one type. Interestingly, patients infected with TcII generally had higher parasite levels but were less likely to have heart disease compared to those with TcVI. The study also found that parasite types TcIII and TcV, previously thought to be rare in Brazil, were present in some patients. Overall, the findings improve understanding of the variety and distribution of T. cruzi types in Brazil and suggest that patient age and parasite type influence parasite levels in the blood. This information may help guide future research on disease progression and treatment.

Leishmania infantum is a parasite that causes a serious disease called visceral leishmaniasis, affecting organs like the liver and spleen. Scientists long thought this parasite reproduced mainly by cloning itself, but recent evidence suggests it can also mate and exchange genetic material inside the sand fly that spreads the disease. This study tested whether parasites of the same genetic type can mate within the sand fly. Researchers created two versions of L. infantum that glowed different colors and were resistant to different drugs. When sand flies were fed a mix of these parasites, some offspring showed both colors and drug resistances, proving that mating and genetic exchange occurred between identical strains. These hybrid parasites had three sets of chromosomes (triploid) and remained stable through their life cycle, including infection in mice. Importantly, the hybrid parasites caused less severe infections in mice, with lower parasite numbers and reduced activity of an enzyme linked to disease severity. This work shows that L. infantum can mate within its natural sand fly vector even between identical strains, producing stable but less aggressive hybrids. Understanding this mating process may help explain how the parasite spreads and adapts in nature.

This study explores how a genetic element called Salmonella genomic island 1 (SGI1), which carries multiple antibiotic resistance genes, spreads between bacteria. SGI1 cannot move on its own but relies on helper plasmids called IncC plasmids to transfer between bacterial cells. These IncC plasmids produce a complex structure called a type IV secretion system (T4SS) that forms a channel for DNA transfer during bacterial mating. SGI1 carries three genes similar to parts of this channel, but their role was unclear. The researchers found that SGI1’s genes are activated by the helper plasmid and produce proteins that can replace or mix with the plasmid’s own channel components. This mixing creates a modified channel that allows SGI1 to transfer more efficiently than the helper plasmid itself. Importantly, one SGI1 protein helps it bypass a natural barrier called entry exclusion, which normally prevents DNA transfer into cells already carrying the helper plasmid. This ability lets SGI1 spread more easily within bacterial populations that already have IncC plasmids. These findings reveal that SGI1 not only uses the helper plasmid’s transfer machinery but also customizes it to boost its own spread, helping explain how multidrug resistance genes can rapidly disseminate among harmful bacteria.

This study investigated how the brain of locusts processes smells by transforming complex, synchronized signals from one brain area (the antennal lobe) into simpler, more selective signals in another area called the mushroom body, which is important for memory. Researchers used computer models based on real locust brain data to explore how changes in the strength of connections (synapses) between these two areas help create specific and reliable responses to different odors. They compared two types of learning rules: one based on the exact timing of nerve impulses (spike-timing dependent plasticity, STDP) and another based on the overall rate of nerve firing (spike-rate dependent plasticity, SRDP). Both types of plasticity made the mushroom body neurons respond more sparsely and specifically to odors, meaning fewer neurons responded but with greater precision. However, the timing-based rule (STDP) was better at maintaining distinct responses to multiple odors and improving the ability to tell similar smells apart. The model showed that plasticity fine-tunes the system to detect synchronized input patterns, which is crucial for accurate odor discrimination. These findings suggest that experience-dependent changes in synaptic strength help stabilize and sharpen odor representations in the brain, supporting learning and memory. The locust olfactory system thus provides a useful model for understanding how neural circuits combine timing and plasticity to process sensory information efficiently.

Natural killer (NK) cells are immune cells that help control viral infections by killing infected cells and producing important signaling proteins called cytokines. Varicella zoster virus (VZV), which causes chickenpox and shingles, can infect human NK cells, but it was unclear how this affects their ability to fight infection. This study used laboratory experiments to grow human NK cells with VZV-infected cells and then tested how well the NK cells could kill target cells and produce cytokines. The researchers found that VZV strongly impaired NK cells’ ability to kill infected cells and produce key cytokines, even in NK cells that were not themselves infected but were exposed to the virus. This loss of function required direct contact between NK cells and VZV-infected cells and was not caused by changes in the NK cells’ surface receptors or by substances released into the surrounding fluid. Further analysis showed that VZV disrupted early steps in the NK cell activation process, effectively paralyzing their response to infected targets. A related virus, herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), was also able to infect and inhibit NK cells, though it affected cytokine production differently. These findings reveal a new way that VZV and HSV-1 evade the immune system by directly blocking NK cell function, which may help the viruses spread and persist in the body. Understanding this interaction could inform future research on viral infections and immune system regulation.

This study explores how the natural variability, or "noise," in the responses of groups of sensory neurons affects their ability to represent information about a stimulus. When the same stimulus is shown repeatedly, neurons respond with some randomness, and this noise can be correlated between pairs of neurons. The researchers asked: how do these noise correlations influence the overall accuracy of the neural population in encoding the stimulus? To answer this, they used a broad mathematical model that makes no assumptions about the specific properties of neurons or their responses. They examined different ways to measure coding accuracy and studied how changing noise correlations impacts these measures. Key findings include: (1) If noise correlations between neuron pairs have opposite signs to their signal correlations (which reflect how similarly neurons respond to changes in the stimulus), then coding accuracy improves compared to when noise is independent. This is called the "sign rule." (2) However, the sign rule is not the only way to improve coding; many diverse noise correlation patterns, including those seen in experiments, can enhance coding even if they violate the sign rule. (3) The best noise correlation patterns always lie on the boundary of the mathematically allowed set of correlations, which is shaped by constraints like fixed individual neuron variability. (4) Under certain conditions, noise correlations can be arranged so that the neural population codes the stimulus as accurately as if there were no noise at all, effectively canceling out noise effects. This noise cancellation is not rare and can occur in large populations. The study also shows that there is a large variety of noise correlation patterns that achieve near-optimal coding, suggesting biological systems might have flexibility in how they organize noise correlations. These results provide a unified understanding of how noise correlations affect neural coding and highlight that optimal coding can arise from many different correlation structures, some of which differ from classical expectations. This work helps clarify why experimentally observed noise correlations sometimes do not follow simple rules and offers a framework for interpreting their role in sensory processing.

Zika virus (ZIKV) is a virus spread by mosquitoes that can cause serious birth defects, including microcephaly, where babies are born with smaller heads and brain problems. While ZIKV outbreaks have been reported in the United States, it was unclear when the virus first affected pregnant women there. This study looked at stored blood samples from 18 mothers in Hawaii who gave birth between 2009 and 2012—six had babies with microcephaly and 12 had healthy babies. Researchers tested the mothers' blood for signs of past or recent ZIKV infection by checking for specific antibodies. They found that some mothers of babies with microcephaly had antibodies indicating ZIKV infection, while most mothers of healthy babies did not. Although the small number of cases meant the results were not statistically definitive, the findings suggest a possible link between ZIKV infection during pregnancy and microcephaly in Hawaii as early as 2009. This timing matches known ZIKV outbreaks in nearby Pacific islands, and it is possible that some mothers were exposed to the virus while traveling. The study highlights the need for larger, future research to better understand ZIKV’s impact on pregnancies in the United States.

This study investigated which bacterial genes help the pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa survive and grow in chronic wound infections, which are long-lasting wounds often difficult to heal. Unlike acute infections that develop quickly and cause severe symptoms, chronic infections can persist for months or years with bacteria living in the wound without spreading widely. Researchers collected many bacterial samples from human chronic wounds and found that many bacteria had lost common traits linked to causing damage, such as producing toxins or forming protective biofilms (clusters of bacteria surrounded by a protective matrix). To understand which bacterial functions are truly important in wounds, the team used a mouse model of chronic wounds and tested many bacterial mutants lacking specific genes. They discovered that most traditional virulence factors and biofilm formation genes were not needed for bacteria to survive in wounds. Instead, genes that help bacteria grow without oxygen (anaerobic growth), manage energy and metabolism, and maintain their cell membranes were critical. Further tests showed that the stresses bacteria face in wounds—such as low oxygen, oxidative damage, and membrane stress—can be mimicked by growing bacteria densely in lab conditions without a host. This suggests that bacteria in wounds mainly deal with stresses caused by their own growth environment rather than direct attacks from the host. The findings challenge the idea that targeting biofilm formation or common virulence factors will be effective treatments for chronic wound infections. Instead, therapies that disrupt bacterial metabolism or stress resistance might be more promising. Overall, this work improves understanding of how P. aeruginosa adapts to chronic wounds and highlights new directions for developing treatments.

This study investigated how the DNA of a bacterial virus called phage Mu is organized when it is integrated into the E. coli bacterial chromosome. Normally, bacterial DNA is tightly packed into loops called supercoiled domains, which help protect and regulate the DNA. The researchers found that the entire Mu genome forms its own stable loop, or 'Mu domain,' held together by specific viral DNA ends and a special DNA site in the middle called SGS. This loop structure depends on both viral proteins, especially MuB, and bacterial proteins known as nucleoid-associated proteins (NAPs) that help shape bacterial DNA. Using genetic tools that measure how close different DNA sites are, the team showed that the Mu ends are brought very close together inside this domain, even though they are far apart in the linear DNA sequence. This domain was seen at different places in the bacterial chromosome and was not found for another phage, lambda, suggesting it is unique to Mu. The Mu domain likely keeps the virus ready to move or 'transpose' within the bacterial genome by maintaining the right DNA shape and proximity of its ends. Additionally, low-level activity of certain viral genes within this domain may provide benefits to the host bacteria, helping the virus remain stable over time. Overall, the study reveals a special DNA loop structure formed by phage Mu in bacteria that supports both viral readiness and potentially host advantages.

This study investigated how zebrafish are able to regrow their amputated fins, focusing on the early step where a special layer of skin cells, called the regeneration epidermis, forms and signals to underlying tissues to start regrowth. Researchers used a genetic approach to find mutations that block this process and identified a key gene called lamb1a, which produces a protein important for the structure and function of this skin layer. After fin amputation, lamb1a is turned on in certain skin cells and helps organize them properly, allowing them to send signals needed for bone-forming cells (osteoblasts) to grow and arrange correctly. The study showed that lamb1a is controlled by a growth factor called Fgf20a and that without lamb1a, the skin cells lose their normal organization, signaling is disrupted, and fin regeneration fails. Interestingly, lamb1a is not needed for normal body growth or simple wound healing, highlighting its specific role in regeneration. The findings reveal that lamb1a acts as a crucial link between growth factor signals and the formation of a signaling skin layer that supports fin regrowth. This work improves understanding of how complex tissue regeneration is controlled in animals capable of regrowing limbs and may inform future regenerative medicine research.

This study focuses on Plasmodium vivax malaria, a common type of malaria that can cause repeated infections called relapses. These relapses happen because the parasite can hide in the liver in a dormant form called hypnozoites, which can activate weeks or months after the initial infection and cause new blood infections. The researchers developed a mathematical model to understand how these dormant parasites behave inside the liver and how they contribute to malaria transmission. They used data from tropical regions to test their model and found that people carry very different numbers of hypnozoites—most have few or none, but some have many, leading to more relapses and greater chances of spreading malaria. The model also showed that standard malaria control methods like mosquito control and treating blood infections reduce transmission, but relapses from hypnozoites make P. vivax harder to control than other malaria types. Importantly, the study predicts that adding drugs like primaquine, which kill hypnozoites in the liver, to treatment plans can greatly reduce relapses and transmission. This is because people with many hypnozoites are more likely to relapse and thus receive treatment that clears both blood and liver infections. The findings highlight the need to target the hidden liver stage of P. vivax to better control and eventually eliminate this form of malaria.

Cells sense mechanical forces through special proteins called Piezo1 ion channels, which open in response to membrane tension and allow ions to flow, creating signals. This study investigated whether Piezo1 channels influence each other’s activity when they are close together in the cell membrane. Using a technique called patch-clamp electrophysiology, researchers measured the number and behavior of Piezo1 channels in small patches of cell membrane from cells with natural (low) and artificially increased (high) levels of Piezo1. They also used computer simulations to model how these channels might be arranged on the membrane. The key finding was that, at both natural and very high densities, Piezo1 channels act independently without affecting each other’s sensitivity to pressure or likelihood of opening. This suggests that Piezo1 channels are spread out or only weakly clustered, allowing cells to detect mechanical forces evenly across their surface. These results help explain how cells maintain consistent mechanical sensing and indicate that any strong clustering of Piezo1 channels would require additional cellular mechanisms beyond the channels themselves.

This study investigates how a protein called Shugoshin-like protein 2 (Sgol2) helps ensure accurate chromosome separation during the first division of egg cells (meiosis I) in mammals. Proper chromosome separation is crucial because errors can lead to eggs with the wrong number of chromosomes, a common cause of miscarriage and developmental problems. The researchers focused on how Sgol2 coordinates several key processes: protecting the connections between sister chromatids (cohesion), regulating the spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) that monitors chromosome attachment, promoting correct chromosome alignment and attachment to spindle fibers (kinetochore-microtubule interactions), and controlling the activity of enzymes called Aurora B/C kinases that modify these attachments. Using mouse egg cells lacking Sgol2 or carrying specific mutations, combined with live imaging and molecular techniques, the team found that Sgol2 protects cohesion by recruiting an enzyme called PP2A to centromeres. Sgol2 also helps turn off the SAC by directly binding to a checkpoint protein Mad2, allowing the cell cycle to progress. Additionally, Sgol2 recruits another protein, MCAK, to kinetochores to limit excessive stretching of chromosome pairs and promotes the formation of stable microtubule attachments by inhibiting Aurora B/C kinase activity at kinetochores. Notably, Sgol2’s ability to regulate these processes depends on different parts of the protein and specific modifications, showing it acts as a central coordinator. These findings reveal that Sgol2 integrates multiple mechanisms to ensure chromosomes are correctly attached and segregated during meiosis I, highlighting its essential role in preventing chromosome segregation errors in egg cells.

Plants use a process called autophagy to protect themselves from infections by breaking down unwanted or harmful components inside their cells. This process involves special proteins, including ATG8 and cargo receptors like Joka2, which help target specific materials for destruction. The study focused on how the potato blight pathogen, Phytophthora infestans, interferes with this defense system. Researchers found that the pathogen produces a protein called PexRD54 that binds strongly to the plant's ATG8CL protein, a key player in autophagy. PexRD54 increases the formation of autophagosomes—structures that carry materials to be degraded—but at the same time, it displaces the plant's cargo receptor Joka2 from ATG8CL. Since Joka2 helps defend the plant by promoting selective autophagy against the pathogen, its removal weakens the plant's defense. Experiments showed that increasing Joka2 levels reduced disease symptoms, but this protective effect was blocked when PexRD54 was present. Overall, the study reveals that PexRD54 hijacks the plant's autophagy machinery to promote infection by outcompeting a defense-related protein, highlighting a sophisticated way pathogens can undermine plant immunity.

This study investigated how certain proteins control the activation of muscle-specific genes during muscle cell development and repair. Normally, gene activity starts when a group of proteins called the Pre-Initiation Complex (PIC) assembles at gene starting points. A key part of this complex is the TFIID protein, which includes TBP (TATA-box binding protein). Previous research suggested that during muscle formation, TBP might be replaced by a related protein called TBP2 (also known as TRF3), which would then activate muscle genes. However, mice lacking TBP2 showed no muscle problems, raising questions about TBP2's role. The researchers tested whether TBP2 is needed for muscle repair in adult mice and found that mice without TBP2 could regenerate muscle normally after injury. They also found that TBP2 is not present in muscle cells or muscle stem cells during differentiation. Instead, TBP and other TFIID components, although reduced in amount, remain present and form complexes essential for turning on muscle genes. When TBP was experimentally reduced in muscle cells, these cells failed to properly develop into muscle fibers, showing that TBP is necessary for muscle gene activation. The study concludes that TBP, not TBP2, is the critical protein for muscle gene expression during muscle cell differentiation and regeneration. This finding clarifies the molecular machinery behind muscle formation and may help understand muscle diseases linked to these proteins.

This study investigated the role of a protein called PALB2, which works with other important proteins (BRCA1 and BRCA2) to repair damaged DNA and prevent cancer. DNA damage repair is crucial because it helps maintain the stability of our chromosomes and prevents mutations that can lead to diseases like breast cancer. PALB2 helps coordinate the repair process by interacting with DNA and other proteins involved in fixing breaks in DNA strands. The researchers identified a specific part of PALB2 that binds directly to DNA and found that changing just four key building blocks (amino acids) in this region reduced the cell’s ability to repair DNA damage by about half. They also discovered that this part of PALB2 can promote important DNA repair steps on its own, even without other proteins usually required for the process. Surprisingly, PALB2 could also work with RNA, suggesting it might have additional roles in DNA repair linked to gene activity. These findings highlight that PALB2’s ability to bind DNA is essential for effective repair of damaged chromosomes, which helps protect cells from becoming cancerous. Understanding how PALB2 works could improve knowledge of cancer development and potentially guide future treatments targeting DNA repair pathways.

This study explored how the movement of proteins inside cells is affected by their electrical charge and the saltiness (ionic strength) of the cell fluid. Proteins need to move around inside cells to interact and carry out important functions, especially in bacteria where active transport is limited. The researchers used specially designed glowing proteins with different surface charges, from very negative to very positive, and measured how fast they moved inside three types of microorganisms: Escherichia coli, Lactococcus lactis, and Haloferax volcanii. They found that in E. coli, proteins with a positive charge moved much more slowly—up to 100 times slower—than negatively charged ones. This slowdown was mainly because positively charged proteins stick to ribosomes, the cell's protein-making machines, which slows their movement. In the other two organisms, this effect was less strong due to higher salt levels that reduce these sticky interactions. The study also showed that how the positive charges are spread on the protein surface matters for movement speed. When cells were exposed to conditions that increase crowding inside the cell, protein movement slowed even more. By analyzing the proteins naturally found in these organisms, the researchers found that most cytoplasmic proteins are negatively charged, likely to avoid slow movement caused by sticking to ribosomes. Interestingly, some bacteria that live inside other cells have mostly positively charged proteins, which raises questions about how they manage protein movement. Overall, the findings suggest that the electrical charge of proteins and their interactions with ribosomes play an important role in controlling how proteins move inside cells, which can influence cell function and protein production.

This study investigated how nerve cells recycle synaptic vesicles (SVs), which are tiny sacs that store and release chemical messengers needed for brain communication. When nerve cells are strongly stimulated, SVs release their contents and their membranes are quickly taken back into the cell through a process called bulk endocytosis, forming large structures called bulk endosomes. These bulk endosomes then help create new SVs, but the exact steps and proteins involved were unclear. The researchers studied nerve cells from mice genetically modified to lack two important proteins, dynamin 1 and dynamin 3, which are usually critical for a common recycling method called clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME). They found that bulk endocytosis still occurred normally or even more than usual without these proteins, and new SVs were still formed from bulk endosomes, although more slowly. Importantly, this SV reformation did not depend on clathrin, another protein thought to be essential for vesicle recycling. Using advanced microscopy and labeling techniques, the team showed that clathrin-coated structures appeared only on the cell surface, not on bulk endosomes, and removing clathrin did not further block SV recovery. These results suggest that during intense nerve activity, nerve cells use a recycling pathway that does not require dynamin 1, dynamin 3, or clathrin to regenerate SVs from bulk endosomes. This finding improves our understanding of how nerve cells maintain communication under high demand and points to alternative mechanisms for vesicle recycling beyond the well-known clathrin-dependent pathway.

Macropinocytosis is a process cells use to take in large amounts of fluid from their surroundings, which helps them gather nutrients and other important molecules. This process involves the cell membrane forming cup-shaped structures called macropinocytic cups, which are pushed outward by a ring of actin protein filaments. However, how cells organize actin into these rings has been unclear. This study used advanced 3D microscopy to closely observe macropinocytosis in a model organism called Dictyostelium. The researchers found that macropinocytic cups form around patches of active signaling molecules, including Ras and PIP3, which appear in the center of the cup. Surrounding these patches is a ring of active SCAR/WAVE protein, which promotes actin polymerization and helps build the cup walls. Importantly, these signaling patches form independently of the actin ring and can grow larger when Ras activity is increased. Most new macropinocytic cups form by splitting from existing ones rather than by folding of membrane ruffles. Similar patterns of signaling and SCAR rings were also seen in related structures like phagocytic cups and basal actin waves. The findings suggest that macropinocytic cups arise through a self-organizing process where patches of active Ras and PIP3 recruit SCAR to their edges, which then drives actin ring formation and cup extension. This new understanding clarifies how cells control the shape and formation of macropinocytic cups, a key step in fluid uptake important for nutrition, immune function, and disease processes.

During early development, animal cells divide rapidly without growing, causing cells to get smaller with each division. The mitotic spindle, a structure made of protein fibers called microtubules, helps separate chromosomes during cell division and must adjust its size to fit the shrinking cells. This study investigated how spindle size changes during development in the frog Xenopus laevis. Researchers created a laboratory system using extracts from embryos at different stages to mimic spindle formation and size seen in living embryos. They found that spindle size decreases as cells get smaller, mainly because of increased activity of a protein called kif2a that destabilizes microtubules. In early large cells, kif2a is kept inactive by another protein, importin α, which binds to kif2a and prevents it from shrinking the spindle. As development proceeds and cells become smaller, importin α moves to the cell membrane, reducing its availability in the cytoplasm and allowing kif2a to become active and reduce spindle size. Changing spindle size in embryos affected how the spindle oriented itself during cell division but did not disrupt chromosome separation. This work shows that spindle size is controlled by a balance between kif2a and importin α, linked to cell size through the distribution of importin α between the cytoplasm and membrane. Understanding this mechanism helps explain how cells coordinate internal structures with changing cell size during development.
